/-!
# Erdős Problem 273
*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/273](https://www.erdosproblems.com/273)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos273

/--
Is there a covering system all of whose moduli are of the form $p-1$ for some primes $p \geq 5$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_273 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ c : StrictCoveringSystem ℤ, ∀ i, ∃ (p : ℕ), p.Prime ∧ 5 ≤ p ∧
    c.moduli i = Ideal.span {↑(p - 1)} := by
  sorry

/--
Is there a covering system all of whose moduli are of the form $p-1$ for some primes $p \geq 3$?
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_273.variants.three : answer(True) ↔ ∃ c : StrictCoveringSystem ℕ, ∀ i, ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ 3 ≤ p ∧
    c.moduli i = Ideal.span {↑(p - 1)} := by
  -- TODO(Paul-Lez): find reference for this and perhaps formalize the proof?
  sorry

end Erdos273

reformulations.difference: The variant uses StrictCoveringSystem ℕ, whose principal-ideal translates are nonnegative arithmetic rays, whereas the source describes congruence classes covering all integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The existence statements are equivalent, preserving the primes and distinct moduli. From an integer covering, replace each residue by its least nonnegative representative modulo n_i = p_i − 1; the resulting rays cover ℕ. Conversely, for a finite natural-number covering, let M be the product of its positive moduli. For any integer z, cover the natural representative of z modulo M. Since each n_i divides M, z belongs to the corresponding integer congruence class. Equality of principal ideals generated by positive natural numbers is equivalent to equality of their generators over both ℕ and ℤ, so strictness is preserved. The exact existential ℕ/ℤ equivalence was proved for every prime cutoff at least three as Review273.nat_int_version_iff in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

review.notes: Both declarations faithfully state their intended claims. The primary source explicitly requires finite coverings with distinct moduli greater than one. Lean checks verified the ideal/congruence correspondence, distinctness of positive generators, impossibility of an empty covering index, and the smallest permitted prime bounds. The source still marks the main question open and credits Selfridge with the affirmative p = 3 variant, matching both categories and answer(True). The scratch file also independently proves the solved variant using a 12-class covering with moduli dividing 360. It compiles successfully; both principal proof checks have no sorryAx dependency.
